entries.5fdec74076ccf00c172fa59a658939f508727231: <div sID="gen15263" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Song.4" sID="Song.4"/> <div eID="gen15263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15264" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15265" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. Jesus Christ, having espoused his church to himself (<reference osisRef="Song.3.11">ch. iii. 11</reference>), highly commends her beauty in the several expressions of it, concluding her fair, all fair, <reference osisRef="Song.4.1-Song.4.5">ver. 1-5</reference> and again, <reference osisRef="Song.4.7">ver. 7</reference>. II. He retires himself, and invites her with him, from the mountains of terror to those of delight, <reference osisRef="Song.4.6">ver. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.4.8">8</reference>. III. He professes his love to her and his delight in her affection to him, <reference osisRef="Song.4.9-Song.4.14">ver. 9-14</reference>. IV. She ascribes all she had that was valuable in her to him, and depends upon the continued influence of his grace to make her more and more acceptable to him, <reference osisRef="Song.4.15-Song.4.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>.
entries.2995cde2fa07f96365bf57db22ca189114897713: <div eID="gen15265" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15264" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Beauty of the Church.</title> <div sID="gen15266" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Behold, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> fair, my love; behold, thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> fair; thou <hi type="italic">hast</hi> doves' eyes within thy locks: thy hair <hi type="italic">is</hi> as a flock of goats, that appear from mount Gilead. <hi type="super">2</hi> Thy teeth <hi type="italic">are</hi> like a flock <hi type="italic">of sheep that are even</hi> shorn, which came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none <hi type="italic">is</hi> barren among them. 3 Thy lips <hi type="italic">are</hi> like a thread of scarlet, and thy speech <hi type="italic">is</hi> comely: thy temples <hi type="italic">are</hi> like a piece of a pomegranate within thy locks. <hi type="super">4</hi> Thy neck <hi type="italic">is</hi> like the tower of David builded for an armoury, whereon there hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thy two breasts <hi type="italic">are</hi> like two young roes that are twins, which feed among the lilies. <hi type="super">6</hi> Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, I will get me to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense. <hi type="super">7</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> all fair, my love; <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no spot in thee. <div eID="gen15266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15267" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A large and particular account of the beauties of the church, and of gracious souls on whom the image of God is renewed, consisting <hi type="italic">in the beauty of holiness.</hi> In general, he that is a competent judge of beauty, whose <hi type="italic">judgment,</hi> we are sure, <hi type="italic">is according to truth,</hi> and what all must subscribe to, he has said, <hi type="italic">Behold, thou art fair.</hi> She had commended him, and called all about her to take notice of his glories; and hereby she recommends herself to him, gains his favour, and, in return for her respects, he calls to all about him to take notice of her graces. Those that honour Christ he will honour, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.30">1 Sam. ii. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen15267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15268" type="x-p"/> 1. He does not flatter her, nor design hereby either to make her proud of herself or to court her praises of him; but, (1.) It is to encourage her under her present dejections. Whatever others thought of her, she was amiable in his eyes. (2.) It is to teach her what to value herself upon, not any external advantages (which would add nothing to her, and the want of which would deprive her of nothing that was really excellent), but upon the comeliness of grace which he had put upon her. (3.) It is to invite others to think well of her too, and to join themselves to her: "Thou art <hi type="italic">my love,</hi> thou lovest me and art beloved of me, and therefore <hi type="italic">thou art fair.</hi>" All the beauty of the saints is derived from him, and they shine by reflecting his light; it is <hi type="italic">the beauty of the Lord our God</hi> that is <hi type="italic">upon us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.17">Ps. xc. 17</reference>. She was espoused to him, and that made her beautiful. <hi type="italic">Uxor fulget radiis mariti</hi>—<hi type="italic">The spouse shines in her husband's rays.</hi> It it repeated, <hi type="italic">Thou art fair,</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Thou art fair,</hi> denoting not only the certainty of it, but the pleasure he took in speaking of it. <div eID="gen15268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15269" type="x-p"/> 2. As to the representation here made of the beauty of the church, the images are certainly very bright, the shades are strong, and the comparisons bold, not proper indeed to represent any external beauty, for they were not designed to do so, but <hi type="italic">the beauty of holiness, the new man, the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible.</hi> Seven particulars are specified, a number of perfection, for the church is enriched with manifold graces by <hi type="italic">the seven spirits</hi> that <hi type="italic">are before the throne,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.4 1Cor.1.5 1Cor.1.7">Rev. i. 4; 1 Cor. i. 5, 7</reference>. <div eID="gen15269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15270" type="x-p"/> (1.) Her <hi type="italic">eyes.</hi> A good eye contributes much to a beauty: <hi type="italic">Thou hast doves' eyes,</hi> clear and chaste, and often cast up towards heaven. It is not the eagle's eye, that can face the sun, but the <hi type="italic">dove's eye,</hi> a humble, modest, mournful eye, that is the praise of those whom Christ loves. Ministers are the church's eyes (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Isa. lii. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">thy watchmen shall see eye to eye</hi>); they must be like <hi type="italic">doves' eyes,</hi> harmless and inoffensive (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">Matt. x. 16</reference>), having their <hi type="italic">conversation in the world in simplicity and godly sincerity.</hi> Wisdom and knowledge are the eyes of the new man; they must be clear, but not haughty, <hi type="italic">not exercised in things too high for us.</hi> When our aims and intentions are sincere and honest, then we have <hi type="italic">doves' eyes,</hi> when we look not unto <hi type="italic">idols</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.18.6">Ezek. xviii. 6</reference>), but have <hi type="italic">our eyes ever towards the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">Ps. xxv. 15</reference>. The <hi type="italic">doves' eyes are within the locks,</hi> which area as a shade upon them, so that, [1.] They cannot fully see. As long as we are here in this world we <hi type="italic">know but in part,</hi> for a hair hangs in our eyes; <hi type="italic">we cannot order our speech by reason of darkness;</hi> death will shortly cut those locks, and then we shall see all things clearly. [2.] They cannot be fully seen, but as the stars through the thin clouds. Some make it to intimate the bashfulness of her looks; she suffers not her eyes to wander, but limits them with her locks. <div eID="gen15270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15271" type="x-p"/> (2.) Her <hi type="italic">hair;</hi> it is compared to <hi type="italic">a flock of goats,</hi> which looked white, and were, on the top of the mountains, like a fine head of hair; and the sight was more pleasant to the spectator because the goats have not only gravity from their beards, but they are <hi type="italic">comely in going</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.29">Prov. xxx. 29</reference>), but it was most pleasant of all to the owner, much of whose riches consisted in his flocks. Christ puts a value upon that in the church, and in believers, which others make no more account of than of their hair. He told his disciples that <hi type="italic">the very hairs of their head were all numbered,</hi> as carefully as men number their flocks (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.30">Matt. x. 30</reference>), and that <hi type="italic">not a hair of their head should perish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.21.18">Luke xxi. 18</reference>. Some by the <hi type="italic">hair</hi> here understand the outward conversation of a believer, which ought to be comely, and decent, and agreeable to the holiness of the heart. The apostle opposes good works, such as become the professors of godliness, to <hi type="italic">the plaiting of the hair,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9-1Tim.2.10">1 Tim. ii. 9, 10</reference>. Mary Magdalen's hair was beautiful when she wiped the feet of Christ with it. <div eID="gen15271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15272" type="x-p"/> (3.) Her <hi type="italic">teeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.2">v. 2</reference>. Ministers are the church's teeth; like nurses, they chew the meat for the babes of Christ. The Chaldee paraphrase applies it to the priests and Levites, who fed upon the sacrifices as the representatives of the people. Faith, by which we feed upon Christ, meditation, by which we ruminate on the word and chew the cud upon what we have heard, in order to the digesting of it, are the teeth of the new man. These are here compared to <hi type="italic">a flock of sheep.</hi> Christ called his disciples and ministers a <hi type="italic">little flock.</hi> It is the praise of teeth to be <hi type="italic">even,</hi> to be white, and kept clean, <hi type="italic">like sheep from the washing,</hi> and to be firm and well fixed in the gums, and not like sheep that cast their young; for so the word signifies which we translate <hi type="italic">barren.</hi> It is the praise of ministers to be even in mutual love and concord, to be pure and clean from all moral pollutions, and to be fruitful, bringing forth souls to Christ, and nursing his lambs. <div eID="gen15272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15273" type="x-p"/> (4.) Her <hi type="italic">lips;</hi> these are compared to <hi type="italic">a thread of scarlet,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.3">v. 3</reference>. Red lips are comely, and a sign of health, as the paleness of the lips is a sign of faintness and weakness; her <hi type="italic">lips</hi> were the colour <hi type="italic">of scarlet,</hi> but thin <hi type="italic">lips, like a thread of scarlet.</hi> The next words explain it: <hi type="italic">Thy speech is comely,</hi> always with grace, <hi type="italic">good,</hi> and <hi type="italic">to the use of edifying,</hi> which adds much to the beauty of a Christian. When we praise God with <hi type="italic">our lips, and with the mouth make confession</hi> of him <hi type="italic">to salvation,</hi> then they are as a <hi type="italic">thread of scarlet.</hi> All our good works and good words must be <hi type="italic">washed in the blood of Christ,</hi> dyed like the <hi type="italic">scarlet thread,</hi> and then, and not till then, they are acceptable to God. The Chaldee applies it to the chief priest, and his prayers for Israel on the day of atonement. <div eID="gen15273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15274" type="x-p"/> (5.) Her <hi type="italic">temples,</hi> or cheeks, which are here compared to <hi type="italic">a piece of a pomegranate,</hi> a fruit which, when cut in two, has rich veins or specks in it, like a blush in the face. Humility and modesty, blushing to lift up our faces before God, blushing at the remembrance of sin and in a sense of our unworthiness of the honour put upon us, will beautify us very much in the eyes of Christ. The blushes of Christ's bride are <hi type="italic">within her locks,</hi> which intimates (says Mr. Durham) that she blushes when no other sees, and for that which none sees but God and conscience; also that she seeks not to proclaim her humility, but modestly covers that too; yet the evidences of all these, in a tender walk, appear and are comely. <div eID="gen15274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15275" type="x-p"/> (6.) Her <hi type="italic">neck;</hi> this is here compared to <hi type="italic">the tower of David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.4">v. 4</reference>. This is generally applied to the grace of faith, by which we are united to Christ, as the body is united to the head by the neck; this <hi type="italic">is like the tower of David,</hi> furnishing us with weapons of war, especially <hi type="italic">bucklers</hi> and <hi type="italic">shields,</hi> as the soldiers were supplied with them out of that tower, for <hi type="italic">faith</hi> is our <hi type="italic">shield</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.16">Eph. vi. 16</reference>): those that have it never want a <hi type="italic">buckler,</hi> for God will compass them <hi type="italic">with his favour as with a shield.</hi> When this <hi type="italic">neck is like a tower,</hi> straight, and stately, and strong, a Christian goes on in his way, and works with courage and magnanimity, and does not hang a drooping head, and he does when faith fails. Some make the <hi type="italic">shields of the mighty men,</hi> that are here said to hang up in <hi type="italic">the tower of David,</hi> to be the monuments of the valour of David's worthies. Their shields were preserved, to keep in remembrance them and their heroic acts, intimating that it is a great encouragement to the saints to hold up their heads, to see what great things the saints in all ages have accomplished and won by faith. In <reference osisRef="Heb.11.1-Heb.11.40">Heb. xi.</reference> we have the <hi type="italic">shields of</hi> the <hi type="italic">mighty men</hi> hung up, the exploits of believers and the trophies of their victories. <div eID="gen15275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15276" type="x-p"/> (7.) Her <hi type="italic">breasts;</hi> these are <hi type="italic">like two young roes that are twins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.5">v. 5</reference>. The church's breasts are both for ornament (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.7">Ezek. xvi. 7</reference>) and for use; they are the <hi type="italic">breasts of her consolation</hi> ( <reference osisRef="Isa.66.11">Isa. lxvi. 11</reference>), as she is said to <hi type="italic">suck the breasts of kings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.60.16">Isa. lx. 16</reference>. Some apply these to the two Testaments; others to the two sacraments, the seals of the covenant of grace; others to ministers, who are to be spiritual nurses to the children of God and to give out to them the <hi type="italic">sincere milk of the word, that they may grow thereby,</hi> and, in order to that, are themselves to <hi type="italic">feed among the lilies</hi> where Christ feeds (<reference osisRef="Song.2.16">ch. ii. 16</reference>), that they may be to the babes of the church as full breasts. Or the breasts of a believer are his love to Christ, which he is pleased with, as a tender husband is with the affections of his wife, who is therefore said to be to him <hi type="italic">as the loving hind and the pleasant roe,</hi> because <hi type="italic">her breasts satisfy him at all times,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">Prov. v. 19</reference>. This includes also his edifying others and communicating grace to them, which adds much to a Christian's beauty. <div eID="gen15276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15277" type="x-p"/> II. The bridegroom's resolution hereupon to retire <hi type="italic">to the mountain of myrrh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.4.6">v. 6</reference>) and there to make his residence. This <hi type="italic">mountain of myrrh</hi> is supposed to signify Mount Moriah, on which the temple was built, where incense was daily burnt to the honour of God. Christ was so pleased with the beauty of his church that he chose this to be his rest for ever; here he will dwell <hi type="italic">till the day break and the shadows flee away.</hi> Christ's parting promise to his disciples, as the representatives of the church, answer to this: <hi type="italic">Lo, I am with you always, even to the end of the world.</hi> Where the ordinances of God are duly administered there Christ will be, and there we must meet him at the door of the tabernacle of meeting. Some make these to be the words of the spouse, either modestly ashamed of the praises given her, and willing to get out of the hearing of them, or desirous to be constant to the holy hill, not doubting but there to find suitable and sufficient succour and relief in all her straits, and there to cast anchor, and wish for the day, which, at the time appointed, would <hi type="italic">break and the shadows flee away.</hi> The holy hill (as some observe) is here called both a <hi type="italic">mountain of myrrh,</hi> which is bitter, and a <hi type="italic">hill of frankincense,</hi> which is sweet, for there we have occasion both to mourn and rejoice; repentance is a bitter sweet. But in heaven it will be all frankincense, and no myrrh. Prayer is compared to incense, and Christ will meet his praying people and will bless them. <div eID="gen15277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15278" type="x-p"/> III. His repeated commendation of the beauty of the spouse (<reference osisRef="Song.4.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art all fair, my love.</hi> He had said (<reference osisRef="Song.4.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou art fair;</hi> but here he goes further, and, in review of the particulars, as of those of the creation, he pronounces <hi type="italic">all very good:</hi> "<hi type="italic">Thou art all fair, my love;</hi> thou art all over beautiful, and there is nothing amiss in thee, and thou hast all beauties in thee; thou art <hi type="italic">sanctified wholly</hi> in every part; <hi type="italic">all things have become new</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.17">2 Cor. v. 17</reference>); there is not only a new face and a new name, but a new man, a new nature; <hi type="italic">there is no spot in thee,</hi> as far as thou art renewed." The spiritual sacrifices must be without blemish. <hi type="italic">There is no spot</hi> but such as is often the spot of God's children, none of the leopard's spots. The church, when Christ shall present it to himself a glorious church, will be altogether <hi type="italic">without spot or wrinkle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.27">Eph. v. 27</reference>.
entries.a778976b86dbca7896eb2554e3404e55ffe581a9: <div eID="gen15278" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love of Christ to the Church.</title> <div sID="gen15279" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Come with me from Lebanon, <hi type="italic">my</hi> spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions' dens, from the mountains of the leopards. <hi type="super">9</hi> Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, <hi type="italic">my</hi> spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck. <hi type="super">10</hi> How fair is thy love, my sister, <hi type="italic">my</hi> spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices! <hi type="super">11</hi> Thy lips, O <hi type="italic">my</hi> spouse, drop <hi type="italic">as</hi> the honeycomb: honey and milk <hi type="italic">are</hi> under thy tongue; and the smell of thy garments <hi type="italic">is</hi> like the smell of Lebanon. <hi type="super">12</hi> A garden inclosed <hi type="italic">is</hi> my sister, <hi type="italic">my</hi> spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thy plants <hi type="italic">are</hi> an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard, <hi type="super">14</hi> Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices: <div eID="gen15279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15280" type="x-p"/> These are still the words of Christ to his church, expressing his great esteem of her and affection to her, the opinion he had of her beauty and excellency, the desire he had of, and the delight he had in, her converse and society. And so ought men to love their wives as Christ loves the church, and takes pleasure in it as if it were spotless and had no fault, when yet it is compassed with infirmity. Now, observe here, <div eID="gen15280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15281" type="x-p"/> I. The endearing names and titles by which he calls her, to express his love to her, to assure her of it, and to engage and excite her love to him. Twice here he calls her <hi type="italic">My spouse</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.4.8">v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.4.11">11</reference>) and three times <hi type="italic">My sister, my spouse,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.9-Song.4.10">v. 9, 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.4.12">12</reference>. Mention was made (<reference osisRef="Song.3.11">ch. iii. 11</reference>) of <hi type="italic">the day of his espousals,</hi> and, after that, she is called his <hi type="italic">spouse,</hi> not before. Note, There is a marriage-covenant between Christ and his church, between Christ and every true believer. Christ calls his church his <hi type="italic">spouse,</hi> and his calling her so makes her so. "I have betrothed thee unto me for ever; and, as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall thy God rejoice over thee." He is not ashamed to own the relation, but, as becomes a kind and tender husband, he speaks affectionately to her, and calls her his <hi type="italic">spouse,</hi> which cannot but strongly engage her to be faithful to him. Nay, because no one relation among men is sufficient to set forth Christ's love to his church, and to show that all this must be understood spiritually, he owns her in two relations, which among men are incompatible, <hi type="italic">My sister, my spouse.</hi> Abraham's saying of Sarah, <hi type="italic">She is my sister,</hi> was interpreted as a denying of her to be his wife; but Christ's church is to him both a <hi type="italic">sister</hi> and a <hi type="italic">spouse,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Matt.12.50">Matt. xii. 50</reference>, a <hi type="italic">sister and mother.</hi> His calling her <hi type="italic">sister</hi> is grounded upon his taking our nature upon him in his incarnation, and his making us partakers of his nature in our sanctification. He clothed himself with a <hi type="italic">body</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">Heb. ii. 14</reference>), and he clothes believers with his <hi type="italic">Spirit</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.17">1 Cor. vi. 17</reference>), and so they become his <hi type="italic">sisters.</hi> They are children of God his Father (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.18">2 Cor. vi. 18</reference>) and so they become his <hi type="italic">sisters;</hi> he that sanctifies, and those that are sanctified, are all of one (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.11">Heb. ii. 11</reference>); and he owns them, and loves them, as his sisters. <div eID="gen15281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15282" type="x-p"/> II. The gracious call he gives her to come along with him as a faithful bride, that must forget her own people and her father's house, and leave all to cleave to him. <hi type="italic">Ubi tu Caius, ibi ego Caia</hi>—<hi type="italic">Where thou Caius art, I Caia will be. Come with me from Lebanon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.8">v. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen15282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15283" type="x-p"/> 1. It is a precept; so we take it, like that (<reference osisRef="Song.2.10">ch. ii. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.2.13">13</reference>), <hi type="italic">Rise up, and come away.</hi> All that have by faith come to Christ must come with Christ, in holy obedience to him and compliance with him. Being joined to him, we must walk with him. This is his command to us daily: "<hi type="italic">Come with me, my spouse;</hi> come with me to God as a Father; come with me onward, heavenward; come forward with me; come up with me; <hi type="italic">come with me from Lebanon, from the top of Amana, from the lions' dens.</hi>" These mountains are to be considered, (1.) As seemingly delightful places. Lebanon is called <hi type="italic">that goodly mountain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.3.25">Deut. iii. 25</reference>. We read of the <hi type="italic">glory of Lebanon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.2">Isa. xxxv. 2</reference>) and its goodly smell, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.6">Hos. xiv. 6</reference>. We read of the pleasant <hi type="italic">dew of Hermon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.133.3">Ps. cxxxiii. 3</reference>) and the <hi type="italic">joy of Hermon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.12">Ps. lxxxix. 12</reference>); and we may suppose the other mountains here mentioned to be pleasant ones, and so this is Christ's call to his spouse to come off from the world, all its products, all its pleasures, to sit loose to all the delights of sense. All those must do so that would come with Christ; they must take their affections off from all present things; yea, though they be placed at the upper end of the world, on <hi type="italic">the top of Amana</hi> and <hi type="italic">the top of Shenir,</hi> though they enjoy the highest satisfactions the creature can propose to give, yet they must <hi type="italic">come away</hi> from them all, and live above the tops of the highest hills on earth, that they may have <hi type="italic">their conversation in heaven. Come from</hi> those mountains, to go along with Christ to the holy mountain, the <hi type="italic">mountain of myrrh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.6">v. 6</reference>. Even while we have our residence on these mountains, yet we must look for them, look above them. Shall we <hi type="italic">lift up our eyes to the hills?</hi> No; <hi type="italic">our help comes from the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.121.1-Ps.121.2">Ps. cxxi. 1, 2</reference>. We must look beyond them, to <hi type="italic">the things that are not seen</hi> (as these high hills are), that <hi type="italic">are eternal.</hi> <hi type="italic">From the tops of Shenir and Hermon,</hi> which were on the other side Jordan, as from Pisgah, they could see the land of Canaan; from this world we must look forward to the better country. (2.) They are to be considered as really dangerous. These hills indeed are pleasant enough, but there are in them <hi type="italic">lions' dens;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">mountains of the leopards,</hi> mountains of prey, though they seem <hi type="italic">glorious and excellent,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.76.4">Ps. lxxvi. 4</reference>. Satan, that <hi type="italic">roaring lion,</hi> in the <hi type="italic">prince of this world;</hi> in the things of it he lies in wait to devour. On the tops of these mountains there are many dangerous temptations to those who would take up their residence in them; and therefore <hi type="italic">come with me from</hi> them; let us not set our hearts upon the things of this world, and then they can do us no hurt. <hi type="italic">Come with me from</hi> the temples of idolaters, and the societies of wicked people (so some understand it); <hi type="italic">come out from among them, and be you separate. Come from</hi> under the dominion of your own lusts, which are as <hi type="italic">lions</hi> and <hi type="italic">leopards,</hi> fierce upon us, and making us fierce. <div eID="gen15283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15284" type="x-p"/> 2. It may be taken as a promise: Thou shalt <hi type="italic">come with me from Lebanon, from the lions' dens;</hi> that is, (1.) "Many shall be brought home to me, as living members of the church, from every point, from Lebanon in the north, Amana in the west, Hermon in the east, Shenir in the south, from all parts, to <hi type="italic">sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Matt.8.11">Matt. viii. 11</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Isa.49.11-Isa.49.12">Isa. xlix. 11, 12</reference>. Some <hi type="italic">from the tops of</hi> these mountains, some of the great men of this world, shall give themselves to Christ. (2.) The church shall be delivered from her persecutors, in due time; though now she <hi type="italic">dwells among lions</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Ps. lvii. 4</reference>), Christ will take her with himself from among their dens. <div eID="gen15284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15285" type="x-p"/> III. The great delight Christ takes in his church and in all believers. He delights in them, <div eID="gen15285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15286" type="x-p"/> 1. As in an agreeable bride, <hi type="italic">adorned for her husband</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Rev. xxi. 2</reference>), who <hi type="italic">greatly desires her beauty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.11">Ps. xlv. 11</reference>. No expressions of love can be more passionate than these here, in which Christ manifests his affection to his church; and yet that great proof of his love, his dying for it, that he might present it to himself a glorious church, goes far beyond them all. A spouse so dearly bought and paid for could not but be dearly loved. Such a price being given for her, a high value must needs be put upon her accordingly; and both together may well set us a wondering at <hi type="italic">the height and depth, and length and breadth, of the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge,</hi> that love in which he <hi type="italic">gave himself for us</hi> and gives himself to us. Observe, (1.) How he is affected towards his spouse: <hi type="italic">Thou hast ravished my heart;</hi> the word is used only here. <hi type="italic">Thou hast hearted me,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Thou has unhearted me.</hi> New words are coined to express the inexpressibleness of Christ's surprising love to his church; and the strength of that love is set forth by that which is a weakness in men, the being so much in love with one object as to be heartless to every thing else. This may refer to that love which Christ had to the chosen remnant, before the worlds were, when <hi type="italic">his delights were with the sons of men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.31">Prov. viii. 31</reference>), that first love, which brought him from heaven to earth, to <hi type="italic">seek and save</hi> them at such vast expense, yet including the complacency he takes in them when he has brought them to himself. Note, Christ's heart is upon his church; so it has appeared all along. His treasure is in it; it is his <hi type="italic">peculiar treasure</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Exod. xix. 5</reference>); and therefore there his heart is also. "Never was love like unto the love of Christ, which made him even mindless of himself, when he emptied himself of his glory, and despised all shame and pain, for our sakes. The wound of love towards us, which he had from eternity in himself, made him neglect all the wounds and reproaches of the cross;" so Bishop Reynolds. Thus let us love him. (2.) What it is that thus affects him with delight. [1.] The regard she has to him: <hi type="italic">Thou hast ravished my heart with one of thy eyes,</hi> those <hi type="italic">doves' eyes,</hi> clear and chaste (which were commended, <reference osisRef="Song.4.1">v. 1</reference>), with one glance of those eyes. Christ is wonderfully pleased with those that look unto him as their Saviour, and through the eye of faith dart their affections to him, above any rival whatsoever, and whose <hi type="italic">eyes are ever towards him;</hi> he is soon aware of the first look of a soul towards him and meets it with his favours. [2.] The ornaments she has from him, that is, the obedience she yields to him, for that is the <hi type="italic">chain of her neck,</hi> the graces that enrich her soul, which are connected as links in chain, the exercise of these graces in a conversation which adorns both herself and the doctrine of Jesus Christ, which she professes to believe (as a gold chain is an ornament to persons of quality), and an entire submission to the commanding power of his love. Having shaken off the <hi type="italic">bands of our neck,</hi> by which we were tied to this world (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.2">Isa. lii. 2</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the yoke of our transgressions,</hi> we are bound with the <hi type="italic">cords of love,</hi> as <hi type="italic">chains of gold,</hi> to Jesus Christ, and our necks are brought under his sweet and easy yoke, to drawn in it. This recommends us to Jesus Christ, for this is that true wisdom which, in his account, is <hi type="italic">an ornament of grace unto the head and chains about the neck,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.9">Prov. i. 9</reference>. [3.] The affection she has for him: <hi type="italic">How fair is thy love!</hi> how beautiful is it! Not only thy love itself, but all the fruits and products of it, its working in the heart, its works in the life. How well does it become a believer thus to love Christ, and what a pleasure does Christ take in it! Nothing recommends us to Christ as this does. <hi type="italic">How much better is thy love than wine,</hi> than all the wine that was poured out to the Lord in the drink-offerings! Hence the fruit of the vine is said to <hi type="italic">cheer God and man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.9.13">Judges ix. 13</reference>. She had said of Christ's love, <hi type="italic">It is better than wine</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.1.2">ch. i. 2</reference>), and now Christ says so of hers; there is nothing lost by praising Christ, nor will he be behindhand with his friends in kindness. [4.] The ointments, the odours wherewith she is perfumed, the gifts and graces of the Spirit, her good works, which are <hi type="italic">an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, well-pleasing to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.4.18">Phil. iv. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">The smell of thy ointment</hi> is better <hi type="italic">than all spices,</hi> such as the queen of Sheba presented to Solomon, camel-loads of them (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.2">1 Kings x. 2</reference>), or, rather, than all the spices that were used in compounding the holy incense which was burned daily on the golden altar. Love and obedience to God are more pleasing to Christ than sacrifice or incense. <hi type="italic">The smell of her garments</hi> too, the visible profession she makes of religion, and relation to Christ, before men, and wherein she appears to the world, this is very grateful to Christ, as <hi type="italic">the smell of Lebanon.</hi> Christ having put upon his spouse the <hi type="italic">white raiment</hi> of his own righteousness (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Rev. iii. 18</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the righteousness of saints</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Rev. xix. 8</reference>), and this perfumed with holy joy and comfort, he is well pleased with it. [5.] Her words, both in her devotion to God and her discourses with men (<reference osisRef="Song.4.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy lips O my spouse! drop as the honeycomb,</hi> drop that which is very sweet, and drop it freely and plentifully. If what God speaks to us be <hi type="italic">sweeter</hi> to us <hi type="italic">than the honey and the honeycomb</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.10">Ps. xix. 10</reference>), what we say to him in prayer and praise shall also be pleasing to him: <hi type="italic">Sweet is thy voice.</hi> And if <hi type="italic">out of a good treasure</hi> in the <hi type="italic">heart</hi> we <hi type="italic">bring forth good things,</hi> if our <hi type="italic">speech be always with grace,</hi> if our <hi type="italic">lips use knowledge aright,</hi> if they <hi type="italic">disperse knowledge,</hi> they then, in Christ's account, even <hi type="italic">drop the honeycomb,</hi> out-drop it. <hi type="italic">Honey and milk</hi> (the two staple commodities of Canaan) <hi type="italic">are under thy tongue;</hi> that is, in thy heart, not only reserved there for thy own use as a sweet morsel for thyself, but ready there for the use of others. In the word of God there is sweet and wholesome nourishment, milk for babes, honey for those that are grown up. Christ is well-pleased with those that are full of his word. <div eID="gen15286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15287" type="x-p"/> 2. As in a pleasant garden. And well may a very great delight be compared to the delight taken in a garden, when the happiness of Adam in innocency was represented by the putting of him into a garden, a garden of pleasure. This comparison is pursued, <reference osisRef="Song.4.12-Song.4.14">v. 12-14</reference>. The church is fitly compared to a <hi type="italic">garden,</hi> to a garden which, as was usual, had <hi type="italic">a fountain</hi> in it. Where Solomon made himself <hi type="italic">gardens</hi> and <hi type="italic">orchards</hi> he made himself <hi type="italic">pools of water</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.5-Eccl.2.6">Eccl. ii. 5, 6</reference>), not only for curiosity and diversion, in water-works, but for use, to <hi type="italic">water the gardens.</hi> Eden was <hi type="italic">well watered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.2.10">Gen. ii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.13.10">xiii. 10</reference>. Observe, (1.) The peculiarity of this garden: It is <hi type="italic">a garden enclosed,</hi> a paradise separated from the common earth. It is appropriated to God; he has <hi type="italic">set it apart for himself;</hi> Israel is God's portion, the lot of his inheritance. It is enclosed for secresy; the saints are God's hidden ones, therefore <hi type="italic">the world knows them not;</hi> Christ walks in his garden unseen. It is enclosed for safety; a hedge of protection is made about it, which all the powers of darkness cannot either find or make a gap in. God's vineyard is <hi type="italic">fenced</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Isa. v. 2</reference>); there is a wall about it, a wall of fire. It has a spring in it, and a fountain, but it is <hi type="italic">a spring shut up</hi> and <hi type="italic">a fountain sealed,</hi> which sends its streams <hi type="italic">abroad</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.16">Prov. v. 16</reference>), but is itself carefully locked up, that it may not by any injurious hand be muddied or polluted. The souls of believers are as <hi type="italic">gardens enclosed;</hi> grace in them is as <hi type="italic">a spring shut up</hi> there in <hi type="italic">the hidden man of the heart,</hi> where the water that Christ gives is <hi type="italic">a well of living water,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.14">John iv. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.38">vii. 38</reference>. The Old-Testament church was <hi type="italic">a garden enclosed</hi> by the partition wall of the ceremonial law. The Bible was then a <hi type="italic">spring shut up</hi> and <hi type="italic">a fountain sealed;</hi> it was confined to one nation; but now the wall of separation is removed, the gospel preached to every nation, and <hi type="italic">in Jesus Christ there is neither Greek nor Jew.</hi> (2.) The products of this garden. It is as the garden of Eden, where <hi type="italic">the Lord God made to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.2.9">Gen. ii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thy plants,</hi> or plantations, <hi type="italic">are an orchard of pomegranates with pleasant fruits,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.13">v. 13</reference>. It is not like <hi type="italic">the vineyard of the man void of understanding,</hi> that was <hi type="italic">all grown over with thorns and nettles;</hi> but here are <hi type="italic">fruits, pleasant fruits, all trees of frankincense,</hi> and <hi type="italic">all the chief spices,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.4.14">v. 14</reference>. Here is a great plenty of fruits and great variety, nothing wanting which might either beautify or enrich this garden, might make it either delightful or serviceable to its great Lord. Every thing here is the best of the kind. Their <hi type="italic">chief spices</hi> were much more valuable, because much more durable, than the choicest of our flowers. Solomon was a great master in botany as well as other parts of natural philosophy; he treated largely of trees (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.33">1 Kings iv. 33</reference>), and perhaps had reference to some specific qualities of the fruits here specified, which made them very fit for the purpose for which he alludes to them; but we must be content to observe, in general, the saints in the church, and graces in the saints, are very fitly compared to these <hi type="italic">fruits and spices;</hi> for, [1.] They are planted, and do not grow of themselves; <hi type="italic">the trees of righteousness</hi> are the <hi type="italic">planting of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa. lxi. 3</reference>); grace springs from an incorruptible seed. [2.] They are precious and of high value; hence we read of the <hi type="italic">precious sons of Zion</hi> and their <hi type="italic">precious faith;</hi> they are <hi type="italic">plants of renown.</hi> [3.] They are pleasant, and of a sweet savour to God and man, and, as strong aromatics, diffuse their fragrancy. [4.] They are profitable and of great use. Saints are the blessings of this earth, and their graces are their riches, with which they trade as the merchants of the east with their spices. [5.] They are permanent, and will be preserved to good purpose, when flowers are withered and good for nothing. Grace, ripened into glory, will last for ever.
entries.8be50540009d35b6e5b6f66dacb0a9b5c323172c: <div eID="gen15287" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15288" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon. <hi type="super">16</hi> Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the spices thereof may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits. <div eID="gen15288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15289" type="x-p"/> These seem to be the words of the spouse, the church, in answer to the commendations which Christ, the bridegroom, had given of her as a pleasant fruitful garden. Is she a garden? <div eID="gen15289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15290" type="x-p"/> I. She owns her dependence upon Christ himself to make this garden fruitful. To him she has an eye (<reference osisRef="Song.4.15">v. 15</reference>) as the <hi type="italic">fountain of gardens,</hi> not only the founder of them, by whom they are planted and to whom they owe their being, but the fountain of them, by which they are watered and to which they own their continuance and well-being, and without whose constant supplies they would soon become like the dry and barren wilderness. To him she gives all the glory of her fruitfulness, as being nothing with out him: <hi type="italic">O fountain of gardens!</hi> fountain of all good, of all grace, do not thou fail me. Does a believer say to the church, <hi type="italic">All my springs are in thee,</hi> in thee, O Zion? (<reference osisRef="Ps.87.7">Ps. lxxxvii. 7</reference>), the church transmits the praise to Christ, and says to him, <hi type="italic">All my springs are in thee;</hi> thou art <hi type="italic">the well of living waters</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.13">Jer. ii. 13</reference>), out of which flow the <hi type="italic">streams of Lebanon,</hi> the river Jordan, which had its rise at the foot of Mount Lebanon, and the waters of the sanctuary, which issued out <hi type="italic">from under the threshold of the house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Ezek. xlvii. 1</reference>. Those that are gardens to Christ must acknowledge him a fountain to them, from whose fulness they receive and to whom it is owing that their souls are as <hi type="italic">a watered garden,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.31.12">Jer. xxxi. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">The city of God</hi> on earth is made <hi type="italic">glad</hi> with the <hi type="italic">river</hi> that flows from this fountain (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.4">Ps. xlvi. 4</reference>), and the new Jerusalem has its <hi type="italic">pure river of water of life proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Rev. xxii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen15290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15291" type="x-p"/> II. She implores the influences of the blessed Spirit to make this garden fragrant (<reference osisRef="Song.4.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Awake, O north wind! and come, thou south.</hi> This is a prayer, 1. For the church in general, that there may be a plentiful effusion of the Spirit upon it, in order to its flourishing estate. Ministers' gifts are <hi type="italic">the spices;</hi> when the Spirit is poured out these flow forth, and then <hi type="italic">the wilderness becomes a fruitful field,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.15">Isa. xxxii. 15</reference>. This prayer was answered in the pouring out of the Spirit on <hi type="italic">the day of pentecost</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.1">Acts ii. 1</reference>), ushered in by a <hi type="italic">mighty wind;</hi> then the apostles, who were bound up before, flowed forth, and were <hi type="italic">a sweet savour to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">2 Cor. ii. 15</reference>. 2. For particular believers. Note, (1.) Sanctified souls are as gardens, gardens of the Lord, enclosed for him. (2.) Graces in the soul are as spices in these gardens, that in them which is valuable and useful. (3.) It is very desirable that the spices of grace should flow forth both in pious and devout affections and in holy gracious actions, that with them we may honour God, adorn our profession, and do that which will be grateful to good men. (4.) The blessed Spirit, in his operations upon the soul, is as the <hi type="italic">north and the south wind,</hi> which <hi type="italic">blows where it listeth,</hi> and from several points, <reference osisRef="John.3.8">John iii. 8</reference>. There is the north wind of convictions, and the south wind of comforts; but all, like the wind, brought <hi type="italic">out of God's treasuries</hi> and <hi type="italic">fulfilling his word.</hi> (5.) The flowing forth of the spices of grace depends upon the gales of the Spirit; he stirs up good affections, and works in us both to will and to do that which is good; it is he that makes manifest the savour of his knowledge by us. (6.) We ought therefore to wait upon the Spirit of grace for his quickening influences, to pray for them, and to lay our souls under them. God has promised to give us his Spirit, but he will for this be enquired of. <div eID="gen15291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15292" type="x-p"/> III. She invites Christ to the best entertainment the garden affords: "<hi type="italic">Let my beloved</hi> then <hi type="italic">come into his garden and eat his pleasant fruits;</hi> let him have the honour of all the products of the garden (it is fit he should), and let me have the comfort of his acceptance of them, for that is the best account they can be made to turn to." Observe, 1. She calls it <hi type="italic">his</hi> garden; for those that are espoused to Christ call nothing their own, but what they have devoted to him and desire to be used for him. When the spices flow forth then it is fit to be called his garden, and not till then. The fruits of the garden are his pleasant fruits, for he planted them, watered them, and gave the increase. What can we pretend to merit at Christ's hands when we can invite him to nothing but what is his own already? 2. She begs he would visit it, and accept of what it produced. The believer can take little pleasure in his garden, unless Christ, the beloved of his soul, come to him, nor have any joy of the fruits of it, unless they redound some way or other to the glory of Christ, and he will think all he has well bestowed upon him.  <chapter eID="Song.4"/> <div eID="gen15292" type="x-p"/>

entries.8b5feb6093fd0bc3528b598ea9ad6f1629980393: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8237"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen12972" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Song.4.1-Song.4.16">So 4:1-16</reference>.<div eID="gen12972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12973" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8237"/>1. Contrast with the bride's state by nature (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Is 1:6</reference>) her state by grace (<reference osisRef="Song.4.1-Song.4.7">So 4:1-7</reference>), "perfect through His comeliness put upon her" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.14">Eze 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.3">Joh 15:3</reference>). The praise of Jesus Christ, unlike that of the world, hurts not, but edifies; as His, not ours, is the glory (<reference osisRef="John.5.44">Joh 5:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.4.10">Re 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.11">11</reference>). Seven features of beauty are specified (<reference osisRef="Song.4.1-Song.4.5">So 4:1-5</reference>) ("lips" and "speech" are but one feature, <reference osisRef="Song.4.3">So 4:3</reference>), the number for perfection. To each of these is attached a comparison from nature: the resemblances consist not so much in outward likeness, as in the combined sensations of delight produced by contemplating these natural objects.<div eID="gen12973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12974" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doves'--</hi>the large melting eye of the Syrian dove appears especially beautiful amid the foliage of its native groves: so the bride's "eyes within her locks" (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.44">Lu 7:44</reference>). Maurer for "locks," has "veil"; but locks suit the connection better: so the Hebrew is translated (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.2">Is 47:2</reference>). The dove was the only bird counted "clean" for sacrifice. Once the heart was "the cage of every unclean and hateful bird." Grace makes the change.<div eID="gen12974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyes--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.6.22">Mt 6:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>; contrast <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28">Mt 5:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.16">1Jo 2:16</reference>). Chaste and guileless ("harmless," <reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">Mt 10:16</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="John.1.47">Joh 1:47</reference>). John the Baptist, historically, was the "turtledove" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.12">So 2:12</reference>), with eye directed to the coming Bridegroom: his Nazarite unshorn hair answers to "locks" (<reference osisRef="John.1.29">Joh 1:29</reference>, 36).<div eID="gen12975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hair ... goats--</hi>The hair of goats in the East is fine like silk. As long hair is her glory, and marks her subjection to man (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.6-1Cor.11.15">1Co 11:6-15</reference>), so the Nazarite's hair marked his subjection and separation unto God. (Compare <reference osisRef="Judg.16.17">Jud 16:17</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.17">2Co 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">Tit 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1Pe 2:9</reference>). Jesus Christ cares for the minutest concerns of His saints (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.30">Mt 10:30</reference>).<div eID="gen12976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12977" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appear from--</hi>literally, "that lie down from"; lying along the hillside, they seem to hang from it: a picture of the bride's hanging tresses.<div eID="gen12977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gilead--</hi>beyond Jordan: there stood "the heap of witness" (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.48">Ge 31:48</reference>). <div eID="gen12978" type="x-p"/>
entries.38b1d8fdfd380782c728f0fb38da3ca9a7c73b2b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8238"/><div sID="gen12979" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8238"/><hi type="bold">2. even shorn--</hi>the Hebrew is translated (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.6.25">1Ki 6:25</reference>), "of one size"; so the point of comparison to teeth is their symmetry of form; as in "came up from the washing," the spotless whiteness; and in "twins," the exact correspondence of the upper and lower teeth: and in "none barren," none wanting, none without its fellow. Faith is the tooth with which we eat the living bread (<reference osisRef="John.6.35">Joh 6:35</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.54">54</reference>). Contrast the teeth of sinners (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Psa 57:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.14">Pr 30:14</reference>); also their end (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.7">Psa 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.30">Mt 25:30</reference>). Faith leads the flock to the washing (<reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zec 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1Co 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.5">Tit 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen12979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none ... barren--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.8">2Pe 1:8</reference>). He who is begotten of God begets instrumentally other sons of God. <div eID="gen12980" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcc1dd1132dbf1914bf00f1fb855073c3f76ca59: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8239"/><div sID="gen12981" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8239"/><hi type="bold">3. thread--</hi>like a delicate fillet. Not thick and white as the leper's lips (type of sin), which were therefore to be "covered," as "unclean" (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.45">Le 13:45</reference>).<div eID="gen12981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12982" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scarlet--</hi>The blood of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.5-Isa.6.9">Is 6:5-9</reference>) cleanses the leprosy, and unseals the lips (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Is 57:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.14.2">Ho 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">He 13:15</reference>). Rahab's scarlet thread was a type of it (<reference osisRef="Josh.2.18">Jos 2:18</reference>).<div eID="gen12982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speech--</hi>not a separate feature from the lips (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.9">Zep 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.6">Col 4:6</reference>). Contrast "uncircumcised lips" (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.12">Ex 6:12</reference>). Maurer and Burrowes translate, "thy mouth."<div eID="gen12983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">temples--</hi>rather, the upper part of the cheek next the temples: the seat of shamefacedness; so, "within thy locks," no display (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.5">1Co 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.15">6, 15</reference>). Mark of true penitence (<reference osisRef="Ezra.9.6">Ezr 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.63">Eze 16:63</reference>). Contrast <reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">Jr 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.7">Eze 3:7</reference>.<div eID="gen12984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12985" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pomegranate--</hi>When cut, it displays in rows seeds pellucid, like crystal, tinged with red. Her modesty is not on the surface, but within, which Jesus Christ can see into. <div eID="gen12985" type="x-p"/>
entries.cbf289018fe9983dcea2c8fe7a430f170d22e0d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8240"/><div sID="gen12986" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8240"/><hi type="bold">4. neck--</hi>stately: in beautiful contrast to the blushing temples (<reference osisRef="Song.4.3">So 4:3</reference>); not "stiff" (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.4">Is 48:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>), as that of unbroken nature; nor "stretched forth" wantonly (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Is 3:16</reference>); nor burdened with the legal yoke (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.14">La 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.10">Ac 15:10</reference>); but erect in gospel freedom (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.2">Is 52:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12987" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tower of David--</hi>probably on Zion. He was a man of war, preparatory to the reign of Solomon, the king of peace. So warfare in the case of Jesus Christ and His saints precedes the coming rest. Each soul won from Satan by Him is a trophy gracing the bride (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.22">Lu 11:22</reference>); (each hangs on Him, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.23">Is 22:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.24">24</reference>); also each victory of her faith. As shields adorn a temple's walls (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.11">Eze 27:11</reference>), so necklaces hang on the bride's neck (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.30">Jud 5:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.16">1Ki 10:16</reference>). <div eID="gen12987" type="x-p"/>
entries.992a6e1bbbc93c7b6aaaeed410f2c2f33bbc53ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8241"/><div sID="gen12988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8241"/><hi type="bold">5. breasts--</hi>The bust is left open in Eastern dress. The breastplate of the high priest was made of "two" pieces, folded one on the other, in which were the Urim and Thummim (lights and perfection). "Faith and love" are the double breastplate (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">1Th 5:8</reference>), answering to "hearing the word" and "keeping it," in a similar connection with breasts (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.27">Lu 12:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.28">28</reference>).<div eID="gen12988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">roes--</hi>He reciprocates her praise (<reference osisRef="Song.2.9">So 2:9</reference>). Emblem of love and satisfaction (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">Pr 5:19</reference>).<div eID="gen12989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12990" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.23.2">Psa 23:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among the lilies--</hi>shrinking from thorns of strife, worldliness, and ungodliness (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.7">Mt 13:7</reference>). Roes feed among, not on the lilies: where these grow, there is moisture producing green pasturage. The lilies represent her white dress (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">Psa 45:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Re 19:8</reference>). <div eID="gen12991" type="x-p"/>
entries.f642f472fce2d7b758634b6e9758c7df67f3c5ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8242"/><div sID="gen12992" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8242"/>6. Historically, the hill of frankincense is Calvary, where, "through the eternal Spirit He offered Himself"; the mountain of myrrh is His embalmment (<reference osisRef="John.19.39">Joh 19:39</reference>) till the resurrection "daybreak." The third Canticle occupies the one cloudless day of His presence on earth, beginning from the night (<reference osisRef="Song.2.17">So 2:17</reference>) and ending with the night of His departure (<reference osisRef="Song.4.6">So 4:6</reference>). His promise is almost exactly in the words of her prayer (<reference osisRef="Song.2.17">So 2:17</reference>), (the same Holy Ghost breathing in Jesus Christ and His praying people), with the difference that she then looked for His visible coming. He now tells her that when He shall have gone from sight, He still is to be met with spiritually in prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.16">Psa 68:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Mt 28:20</reference>), until the everlasting day break, when we shall see face to face (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.10">1Co 13:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen12992" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4b7f38295ad0144a377d80965e4635148879676: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8243"/><div sID="gen12993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8243"/>7. Assurance that He is going from her in love, not in displeasure (<reference osisRef="John.16.6">Joh 16:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.16.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen12993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12994" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all fair--</hi>still stronger than <reference osisRef="Song.1.15">So 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.4.1">So 4:1</reference>.<div eID="gen12994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12995" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no spot--</hi>our privilege (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.27">Ep 5:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.10">Col 2:10</reference>); our duty (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.17">2Co 6:17</reference>; Jude 23; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.27">Jas 1:27</reference>). <div eID="gen12995" type="x-p"/>
entries.8afd94eb07149702a739eda81285f7014517f4a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8244"/><div sID="gen12996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8244"/>8. Invitation to her to leave the border mountains (the highest worldly elevation) between the hostile lands north of Palestine and the Promised Land (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.10">Psa 45:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.13">Php 3:13</reference>).<div eID="gen12996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Amana--</hi>south of Anti-Libanus; the river Abana, or Amana, was near Damascus (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.12">2Ki 5:12</reference>).<div eID="gen12997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shenir--</hi>The whole mountain was called Hermon; the part held by the Sidonians was called Sirion; the part held by the Amorites, Shenir (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.9">De 3:9</reference>). Infested by the devouring lion and the stealthy and swift leopard (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.4">Psa 76:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.11">Ep 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.8">1Pe 5:8</reference>). Contrasted with the mountain of myrrh, &c. (<reference osisRef="Song.4.6">So 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>); the good land (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.9">Is 35:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with me--</hi>twice repeated emphatically. The presence of Jesus Christ makes up for the absence of all besides (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.29">Lu 18:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.18.30">30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.10">2Co 6:10</reference>). Moses was permitted to see Canaan from Pisgah; Peter, James, and John had a foretaste of glory on the mount of transfiguration. <div eID="gen12999" type="x-p"/>
entries.5032f8733898d638ae04c1b76a9058575ff13f29: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8245"/><div sID="gen13000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8245"/><hi type="bold">9. sister ... spouse--</hi>This title is here first used, as He is soon about to institute the Supper, the pledge of the nuptial union. By the term "sister," carnal ideas are excluded; the ardor of a spouse's love is combined with the purity of a sister's (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.5">Is 54:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Mark.3.35">Mr 3:35</reference>).<div eID="gen13000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one--</hi>Even one look is enough to secure His love (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.40-Luke.23.43">Lu 23:40-43</reference>). Not merely the Church collectively, but each one member of it (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.10">Mt 18:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.7">Lu 15:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.32">24, 32</reference>).<div eID="gen13001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chain--</hi>necklace (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.3">Is 62:3</reference>; Mal 3:17), answering to the "shields" hanging in the tower of David (<reference osisRef="Song.4.4">So 4:4</reference>). Compare the "ornament" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.4">1Pe 3:4</reference>); "chains" (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.9">Pr 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22">3:22</reference>). <div eID="gen13002" type="x-p"/>
entries.f926a55c72fad19b1213c767b181c8f6d48f6ac2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8246"/><div sID="gen13003" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8246"/><hi type="bold">10. love--</hi>Hebrew, "loves"; manifold tokens of thy love.<div eID="gen13003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">much better--</hi>answering to her "better" (<reference osisRef="Song.1.2">So 1:2</reference>), but with increased force. An Amoebean pastoral character pervades the Song, like the classic Amoebean idylls and eclogues.<div eID="gen13004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wine--</hi>The love of His saints is a more reviving cordial to Him than wine; for example, at the feast in Simon's house (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.36">Lu 7:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.47">47</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.32">Joh 4:32</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.10.7">Zec 10:7</reference>).<div eID="gen13005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smell of ... ointments than all spices--</hi>answering to her praise (<reference osisRef="Song.1.3">So 1:3</reference>) with increased force. Fragrant, as being fruits of His Spirit in us (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.22">Ga 5:22</reference>). <div eID="gen13006" type="x-p"/>
entries.39e6ca402a73c695f63812f1a35d4354c20e1f9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8247"/><div sID="gen13007" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8247"/><hi type="bold">11. drop--</hi>always ready to fall, being full of honey, though not always (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.19">Pr 10:19</reference>) actually dropping (<reference osisRef="Song.5.13">So 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">De 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.34">Mt 12:34</reference>).<div eID="gen13007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honeycomb--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.5.3">Pr 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.16.24">16:24</reference>).<div eID="gen13008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">under thy tongue--</hi>not always on, but under, the tongue, ready to fall (<reference osisRef="Ps.55.21">Psa 55:21</reference>). Contrast her former state (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.3">Psa 140:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.13">Ro 3:13</reference>). "Honey and milk" were the glory of the good land. The change is illustrated in the penitent thief. Contrast <reference osisRef="Matt.27.44">Mt 27:44</reference> with <reference osisRef="Luke.23.39">Lu 23:39</reference>, &c. It was literally with "one" eye, a sidelong glance of love "better than wine," that he refreshed Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Song.4.9">So 4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.4.10">10</reference>). "To-day shalt thou be with Me (compare <reference osisRef="Song.4.8">So 4:8</reference>) in Paradise" (<reference osisRef="Song.4.12">So 4:12</reference>), is the only joyous sentence of His seven utterances on the cross.<div eID="gen13009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smell of ... garments--</hi>which are often perfumed in the East (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.8">Psa 45:8</reference>). The perfume comes from Him on us (<reference osisRef="Ps.133.2">Psa 133:2</reference>). We draw nigh to God in the perfumed garment of our elder brother (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.27">Ge 27:27</reference>; see Jude 23).<div eID="gen13010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lebanon--</hi>abounding in odoriferous trees (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.5-Hos.14.7">Ho 14:5-7</reference>). <div eID="gen13011" type="x-p"/>
entries.51463d3d4fc2a7cab85dbbd3c6205d32c54b28a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8248"/><div sID="gen13012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8248"/>12. The Hebrew has no "is." Here she is distinct from the garden (<reference osisRef="Song.5.1">So 5:1</reference>), yet identified with it (<reference osisRef="Song.4.16">So 4:16</reference>) as being one with Him in His sufferings. Historically the Paradise, into which the soul of Jesus Christ entered at death; and the tomb of Joseph, in which His body was laid amid "myrrh," &c. (<reference osisRef="Song.4.6">So 4:6</reference>), situated in a nicely kept garden (compare "gardener," <reference osisRef="John.20.15">Joh 20:15</reference>); "sealed" with a stone (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.66">Mt 27:66</reference>); in which it resembles "wells" in the East (<reference osisRef="Gen.29.3">Ge 29:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.8">8</reference>). It was in a garden of light Adam fell; in a garden of darkness, Gethsemane, and chiefly that of the tomb, the second Adam retrieved us. Spiritually the garden is the gospel kingdom of heaven. Here all is ripe; previously (<reference osisRef="Song.2.13">So 2:13</reference>) it was "the tender grape." The garden is His, though He calls the plants hers (<reference osisRef="Song.4.13">So 4:13</reference>) by His gift (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Is 61:3</reference>, end).<div eID="gen13012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spring ... fountain--</hi>Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="John.4.10">Joh 4:10</reference>) sealed, while He was in the sealed tomb: it poured forth its full tide on Pentecost (<reference osisRef="John.7.37-John.7.39">Joh 7:37-39</reference>). Still He is a sealed fountain until the Holy Ghost opens it to one (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1Co 12:3</reference>). The Church also is "a garden enclosed" (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1">Is 5:1</reference>, &c.). Contrast <reference osisRef="Ps.80.9-Ps.80.12">Psa 80:9-12</reference>. So "a spring" (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">Is 27:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">58:11</reference>); "sealed" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.30">Ep 4:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>). As wives in the East are secluded from public gaze, so believers (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.3">Psa 83:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">Col 3:3</reference>). Contrast the open streams which "pass away" (<reference osisRef="Job.6.15-Job.6.18">Job 6:15-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.17">2Pe 2:17</reference>). <div eID="gen13013" type="x-p"/>
entries.30f6eb23959585528a19a8ab3348c89de3f2bc8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8249"/><div sID="gen13014" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8249"/><hi type="bold">13. orchard--</hi>Hebrew, "a paradise," that is, a pleasure-ground and orchard. Not only flowers, but fruit trees (<reference osisRef="John.15.8">Joh 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.11">Php 1:11</reference>).<div eID="gen13014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">camphire--</hi>not camphor (<reference osisRef="Song.1.14">So 1:14</reference>), hennah, or cypress blooms. <div eID="gen13015" type="x-p"/>
entries.48c1375ad5bb862cd5d2aff4e50edc0181a2f0c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8250"/><div sID="gen13016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8250"/><hi type="bold">14. calamus--</hi>"sweet cane" (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.23">Ex 30:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">Jr 6:20</reference>).<div eID="gen13016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">myrrh and aloes--</hi>Ointments are associated with His death, as well as with feasts (<reference osisRef="John.12.7">Joh 12:7</reference>). The bride's ministry of "myrrh and aloes" is recorded (<reference osisRef="John.19.39">Joh 19:39</reference>). <div eID="gen13017" type="x-p"/>
entries.aead81984db2179fce1e23cbefc9bd1262e963f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8251"/><div sID="gen13018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8251"/><hi type="bold">15. of--</hi>This pleasure-ground is not dependent on mere reservoirs; it has a fountain sufficient to water many "gardens" (plural).<div eID="gen13018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">living--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jr 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.4.13">Joh 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.4.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.38">7:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.7.39">39</reference>).<div eID="gen13019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Lebanon--</hi>Though the fountain is lowly, the source is lofty; fed by the perpetual snows of Lebanon, refreshingly cool (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.14">Jr 18:14</reference>), fertilizing the gardens of Damascus. It springs upon earth; its source is heaven. It is now not "sealed," but open "streams" (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">Re 22:17</reference>). <div eID="gen13020" type="x-p"/>
entries.884c27f6813a4b2cf88e46179fba13be89b3af79: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8252"/><div sID="gen13021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8252"/><hi type="bold">16. Awake--</hi>literally, "arise." All besides is ready; one thing alone is wanted--the breath of God. This follows rightly after His death (<reference osisRef="Song.6.12">So 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.1-Acts.2.4">Ac 2:1-4</reference>). It is His call to the Spirit to come (<reference osisRef="John.14.16">Joh 14:16</reference>); in <reference osisRef="John.3.8">Joh 3:8</reference>, compared to "the wind"; quickening (<reference osisRef="John.6.63">Joh 6:63</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.9">Eze 27:9</reference>). Saints offer the same prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.6">Psa 85:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.2">Ha 3:2</reference>). The north wind "awakes," or arises strongly, namely, the Holy Ghost as a reprover (<reference osisRef="John.16.8-John.16.11">Joh 16:8-11</reference>); the south wind "comes" gently, namely, the Holy Ghost as the comforter (<reference osisRef="John.14.16">Joh 14:16</reference>). The west wind brings rain from the sea (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.44">1Ki 18:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.45">45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.54">Lu 12:54</reference>). The east wind is tempestuous (<reference osisRef="Job.27.21">Job 27:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.8">Is 27:8</reference>) and withering (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.23">Ge 41:23</reference>). These, therefore, are not wanted; but first the north wind clearing the air (<reference osisRef="Job.37.22">Job 37:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.23">Pr 25:23</reference>), and then the warm south wind (<reference osisRef="Job.37.17">Job 37:17</reference>); so the Holy Ghost first clearing away mists of gloom, error, unbelief, sin, which intercept the light of Jesus Christ, then infusing spiritual warmth (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2Co 4:6</reference>), causing the graces to exhale their odor.<div eID="gen13021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Let my beloved, &c.--</hi>the bride's reply. The fruit was now at length ripe; the last passover, which He had so desired, is come (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.7">Lu 22:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.16">15, 16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.15.18">18</reference>), the only occasion in which He took charge of the preparations.<div eID="gen13022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his--</hi>answering to Jesus Christ's "My." She owns that the garden is His, and the fruits in her, which she does not in false humility deny (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Psa 66:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.21.19">Ac 21:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.10">1Co 15:10</reference>) are His (<reference osisRef="John.15.8">Joh 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.11">Php 1:11</reference>). <chapter eID="Song.4"/>

entries.d490f8c77ddf6595d442fb3d244cbde915a49df8: <div eID="gen25987" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25988" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25989" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25989" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25988" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25990" type="x-p"/> The bridegroom's description of his bride, her person, her accomplishments, her chastity, and her general excellence, vv. 1-16. <div eID="gen25990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25991" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25992" type="x-p"/> Thou hast doves' eyes within thy locks - Perhaps this refers rather to a sort of veil worn by many of the Eastern women, but especially in Egypt. It is a species of black cloth made of the hair of some animal, probably the black goat; is suspended from the head by silken cords, one of which comes from the crown of the head, down the forehead, to the upper part of the nose, just under the eyes, at which place the veil begins; for the forehead and the eyes are uncovered, except the cord above mentioned, which is ornamented with gold, silver, and precious stones, according to the circumstances of the wearer. This partial veil not only covers all the face, the eyes and forehead excepted, but the neck also, and hangs loosely down over the bosom. One of them, lately brought from Egypt, now lies before me. <div eID="gen25992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25993" type="x-p"/> But the clause, within thy locks, מבעד למתך mibbaad letsammathech, is not well translated, either by ourselves or by the versions. Jerome's translation is an indication of the meaning: Absque eo quod intrinsecus latet; without that, or independently of that, which lies hidden within. The Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic have, besides thy silence. Calmet contends that none of these gives the true meaning, and that the word tmu tsemath has not the meaning of hair or locks wherever it occurs, and has quite a different meaning in <reference osisRef="Isa.47.2">Isa 47:2</reference>. St. Jerome on this place expresses himself thus: Nolentibus gui interpretati sunt transferre nomen quod in Sancta Scriptura sonat turpitudinem - Ergo Ktmu tsammathech, quod Aquila posuit, verenda mulieris appellanatur cujus etymologia apud eos sonat sitiens tuus. Calmet translates: Vous etes toute belle, won amie; vous etes toute belle: vos yeux sont des yeux de colombe; sans ce que la pudeur et la modestie tiennent cache. I leave the translation of these to the learned reader. See another description under <reference osisRef="Sol.4.7">Sol 4:7</reference> (note). <div eID="gen25993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25994" type="x-p"/> As a flock of goats - Because it was black and sleek, as the hair of the goats of Arabia and Palestine is known to be; which, with its fine undulation, is supposed to bear some resemblance to the curls or plaits of a woman's tresses. The mountains of Gilead were beyond Jordan, on the frontiers of Arabia Deserta.
