<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="4" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. IV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 15. & 5. 12.</ns0:note> BEhold <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">These and the following words are evidently spoken by the Bridegroom to, and concerning, his Spouse.</ns0:note>, thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> fair <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Not in thy self, but by my beauty, being cloathed with my Righteousness, and ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />orned with all the Graces of my Spirit, which I acknowledg to be in thee.</ns0:note>, my love, behold, thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> fair <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">He repeats it both to confirm the Truth of his As<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sertion, and to shew the sincerity and fervency of his Affection to her.</ns0:note>, thou <ns0:hi>hast</ns0:hi> doves eyes <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Thou art harmless, chaste, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> as appears by thine Eyes, which commonly discover the temper of the Mind or Person. See more of this Phrase <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 1. 15. And whereas the beauty of the Spouse is here described in her several parts, we need not labour much about the Application of each particular to some distinct Member or Grace of the Church, this being the chief design of this description of a Bride which is beautiful in all points, to shew that compleatness and absolute perfection which the Church hath in part received, and shall more fully receive from Christ in the future Life. Yet because the Church is a Body, consisting of di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers Members, and enriched with variety of Gifts and Graces, I know no reason, but the several parts of this description may have a more special regard to one or other of them. And so her <ns0:hi>Eyes</ns0:hi> may here note either 1. Her Teachers, who are <ns0:hi>instead of Eyes</ns0:hi> to her, as the Phrase is, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 10. 31. whence they are called <ns0:hi>Seers</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Guides,</ns0:hi> &c. Or 2. The disposition of her Mind or Heart, which is compared to the <ns0:hi>Eye, Mat.</ns0:hi> 6. 22, 23. and is oft discerned in the Eye.</ns0:note> within thy locks <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which being decently composed make the Eyes appear more amiable, withal this intimates the modesty of her Looks: her Eyes are not wanton, and wandring, or lofty, but sober, and humble, and confined within their proper bounds, looking di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rectly upon her Husband, not looking asquint upon other Lovers, nor minding other Gods or Christs. If the <ns0:hi>Eyes</ns0:hi> signifie Teachers, the <ns0:hi>Locks</ns0:hi> may note the People assembled together to hear their Teachers, to whom they are a great Ornament when they thrive by his Teaching.</ns0:note>: thy hair <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The Hair of thine Head, which is a great Or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nament to the Female Sex, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11. 15. This <ns0:hi>Hair</ns0:hi> may signifie either 1. The inward Thoughts and Meditations: Or rather 2. The outward Conversation, and visible fruits of Holiness, which do greatly adorn the Professors and Profession of Religion, as Hair doth the Head, as is implied 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 2. 9, 10. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3. 3, 4, 5.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> as a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 6. 5, 6.</ns0:note> flock of goats <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Which are comely and orderly in going, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 30. 29, 31. and afford a goodly prospect. Or rather, <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> the hair (which word is here to be understood, as appears both from the comparison itself, and from divers places where <ns0:hi>Goats</ns0:hi> are put for <ns0:hi>goats hair;</ns0:hi> as it is in the Hebrew Text, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 25. 4. & 26. 7. & 35. 26.) of <ns0:hi>a flock of goats,</ns0:hi> which in these parts was of extraordinary length, and thick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, and softness, and comeliness, and much more like to the Hair of a Man or Woman than the Hair of our Goats is, as is evident both from Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 27. 16. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 13. and from the Testimony of other ancient Writers, as <ns0:hi>Apuleius, Martial,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> of,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> that ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pear from <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That feeding there, or coming down thence, or going up thi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, shew themselves evidently to those who stand below it, or near them. Or, as it is rendred in our margent, and by others, <ns0:hi>that eat,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>graze of,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>upon.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> mount Gilead <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which he mentions as a very fruitful place, and fit for the breeding of all sorts of cattle, as is manifest from <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 32. 1. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 50. 19. <ns0:hi>Mich.</ns0:hi> 7. 14. and especially of Goats, partly be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause it was an hilly and woody country, and partly because it a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bounded with rosinous, and oily, and gummy Trees, as appears from <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 37. 25. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 8. 22. & 46. 11. wherewith the Goats are much delighted, as <ns0:hi>Dioscorides</ns0:hi> observes. And some affirm that the Hair of these Goats was commonly of a yellow colour, as may seem probable from 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 13, 16. compared with 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 16. 12. and from <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 7. 5. which also was in ancient times esteemed a beau<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty in Men or Women, as the Learned know.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Thy teeth <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> like a flock <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Numerous and placed in due order.</ns0:note> of <ns0:hi>sheep</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Which is here fitly supplied out of <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 6. 6. where it is expressed. Smooth and even, as also clean and white, whereas unshorn sheep retain much filth in their wool, even after their washing.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>that are</ns0:hi> e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven shorn <ns0:hi>m,</ns0:hi> which came up from the washing: where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />of every one bear twins <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which seems to note the two rows of Teeth, like Twins, one directly answering to the other; which is a great part of the Beauty or comeliness be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />longing to the Teeth. Nor let any wonder to hear of <ns0:hi>sheep bearing Twins;</ns0:hi> for that there were many such in the Eastern Countries is apparent, not only from holy Scripture, but also from the express Testimony of <ns0:hi>Aristotle,</ns0:hi> and other ancient Writers.</ns0:note>, and none <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> barren among them <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Not one Tooth is lacking. By the <ns0:hi>Teeth</ns0:hi> some understand the Teachers, which may be compared to Teeth, because they prepare, and as it were chew spiritual Food for the People, and to such Teeth as are here described for their great number and excellent order, and for that purity and fruitfulness which is required of them: others understand some gracious qualification or action of the faithful, either their Faith, which is compared to eating, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 6. 41, &c. and elsewhere, which also purifies the Heart and Life, and pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duceth good works in abundance; or their Meditation or study of God, and of his word, whereby, like the clean Beasts under the Law, they chew the cud; which also much promotes their puri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty and fertility. But, as I said on the first verse, there is no need of a distinct Application of every particular, as it is in Parables where many things are added for decency, which belong not to the main scope, and therefore are neglected in the interpretation of them. The scope of this place is onely to set forth the Churches perfection and beauty by the resemblance of a beautiful Woman, and one part of beauty consists in the colour and order of the teeth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:560" />3 Thy lips <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> like a thread of scarlet <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Fine, and smooth, and soft, and round, and red, in which the beauty of the Lips consisteth.</ns0:note>, and thy speech <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> comely <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Which is added partly as ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther ingredient of an amiable Person; and partly to explain the foregoing Metaphor. The Communication or Discourse of Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lievers is edifying, and comfortable, and acceptable to God, and to serious men. Compare <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 45. 2. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 4. 6.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 6. 7.</ns0:note> thy temples <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Under which doubtless he comprehends the cheeks, which are joined to them, and in which a great part of beauty lies, which therefore would not have been omitted in this description.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> like a piece of a pomgranate <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">In which there is a lovely mixture of red and white. This may note both the Churches beauty, and her modesty, which sheweth itself by blushes in those parts when she hath falln into any sin, as the highest Believers in this World somtimes do.</ns0:note> within thy locks <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">A further evidence both of beauty and modesty. See on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Thy neck <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This may seem to represent the Grace of Faith, by which we are united to Christ, as the Body is to the Head by the Neck, and through which Christians receive their spiritual Food, and conse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently their strength and ability for Action.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> like the tower of David <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Round, and smooth, and white, long, and streight, and upright, firm, and strong; and moreover adorned with chains of Gold or Pearl, or the like Ornaments. All which things as they set forth the beauty of the Neck, so they may signifie the various excellencies and uses of Faith. By this <ns0:hi>Tower</ns0:hi> he understands either 1. The strong hold of <ns0:hi>Sion,</ns0:hi> of which see 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 5. 9. Or rather 2. Some other Tower built by <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> when he repaired, and enlarged, and for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tified his Royal City, 1 <ns0:hi>Chr.</ns0:hi> 11. 8. and used by him as an Armo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry. See <ns0:hi>Neh.</ns0:hi> 3. 19, 25, 26, 27.</ns0:note> built for an armory, whereon there hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either 1. Such as are fit and reserved for the use of mighty Men. Or 2. Such as had been used either by themselves, or by their Enemies, from whom they took them by force, and were hung up there as Trophies or Monuments of Victory. Which is added to shew that the Church is not only beautiful and glorious, but also strong and victorious over all her Enemies, and to intimate the great power and exploits of Faith, of which read <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11. and which is compared to a <ns0:hi>shield,</ns0:hi> Eph. 6. 16. A <ns0:hi>thousand</ns0:hi> is here put indefinitely for a great number.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 7. 3.</ns0:note> Thy two breasts <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Another part in which beauty consists, <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 16. 7. By which some understand the two Testaments, or the two Sacraments: but these are rather Christs than the Churches Breasts. Others, the Churches servent Love to Christ, and to all the Saints, for the Breasts signifie Love, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 5. 19. <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 1. 13. Others her fruit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness, both in good Works, and in bringing up Children unto Christ, like a Nurse with her Breasts. But the following simili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tude seemeth not to respect the use of the Breasts, or the Love which is signified or manifested by them, but their comeliness. And therefore this is generally to be understood of the Churches Beauty in all parts, as hath been said.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> like two young roes that are twins, which feed among the lillies <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In the fields where Lilies grew, as is evident both from <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 6. 28. where they are called <ns0:hi>the Lillies of the field,</ns0:hi> and from other Scriptures, and from the Testimony of other Writers. The <ns0:hi>Lillies</ns0:hi> being white and swel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling, and the <ns0:hi>Roes</ns0:hi> of a reddish colour, and their Bodies being hid from sight by the Lillies, their Heads only appearing above them, bear some resemblance to the red nipples appearing in the top of the lillie white Breasts. But we must remember that this Book is a sacred Pastoral, and the Bridegroom is represented as a Shepherd and the Bride as a country<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>Maid, and therefore such similitudes are used as are agreeable to Persons of that Quality, and such are usual in prophane Writers of this kind, as the learned have ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served. They are compared to <ns0:hi>Roes</ns0:hi> for their loveliness, of which see <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 5. 19. to <ns0:hi>young</ns0:hi> ones for their smallness, which in breasts is a beauty; to <ns0:hi>Twins</ns0:hi> for their exact likeness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 2. 17.</ns0:note> Until the day <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> breath.</ns0:note> break, and the shadows flee away <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">These words are uttered by the Bride, <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 2. <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17. and here returned by the Bridegroom as an Answer to that Request. And this place may be understood either 1. Of the day of the Gospel, when all legal shadows shall vanish: Or 2. Of the day of Glory, or of the general Resurrection, when all manner of shadows and Ordinances shall cease. Till which time either the Spouse <ns0:hi>feeds a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mong Lillies,</ns0:hi> as was now said, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. or the Bridegroom <ns0:hi>gets</ns0:hi> him <ns0:hi>to the mountains,</ns0:hi> &c. as it follows. For the words are by most joined with the foregoing, and by some with the following clause.</ns0:note>, I will get me to the mountain of myrrhe, and to the hill of frankincense <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther 1. To the Temple at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> which is oft and fitly ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed by the name of a <ns0:hi>mountain</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>hill,</ns0:hi> because it was built upon a Mountain, and which may be called <ns0:hi>a Mountain of Myrrhe</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>frankincense,</ns0:hi> because of the abundance of Myrrhe and Frankincense which was there used and offered; in which place the Church was to feed, and Christ would continue his presence until the dawning of the Gospel-day. Or 2. To my Church upon Earth, which was typified by the Mountain of <ns0:hi>Moriah,</ns0:hi> and the Temple upon it, and which in Prophetical Writings is called a <ns0:hi>Mountain,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 2. 2, 3. <ns0:hi>Mich.</ns0:hi> 4. 1, 2. & elsewhere, & which may well be call'd a <ns0:hi>Mountain of Myrrhe & Frankincense,</ns0:hi> both for the acceptable services which are there offer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to God, and for the precious Gifts, and Graces, and Comforts of the Holy Spirit, which are of a sweet smelling savour to God and Men, and which there, and there only, are poured sorth. Thus Christ directs his Bride, to wit, particular Believers, where they may find and enjoy him, namely in his Church and Ordinances.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 5. 27.</ns0:note> Thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> all fair <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">It is needless to mention the several beauties of all thy parts, for in one word thou art wholly beautiful, and it may be said more truly of thee than it was of <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 14. 25. that from the sole of thy Foot to the crown of thy Head there is no blemish in thee.</ns0:note>, my love, <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> no spot in thee <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Which is not to be understood simply and absolutely, as if the People of God were really perfect, and free from all sin, but either 1. Comparatively, no such spot or blemish as is in wicked Men, or, as is inconsistent with true Grace, of which <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> speaks, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 5. Or 2. In regard of Gods gracious acceptation, in which respect he is said, not to <ns0:hi>behold iniquity in</ns0:hi> Jacob, <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 23. 21. God doth not look upon them with a severe Eye, as they are in themselves, but in and through Christ, in whom he accepts them as if they were perfect, partly because it is their chief design, de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sire, and endeavour to be so, and partly because Christ hath un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dertaken to make them so, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 5. 25, 27. and they shall one day be such.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Come with me <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Unto the Mountains of Myrrhe, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> mentioned <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 6.</ns0:note> from Lebanon <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">A known Mountain in the North of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> which is somtimes men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioned as a pleasant and glorious place, as <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 5. 15. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 35. 2. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 14. 6, &c. in regard of its goodly Cedars; and somtimes as a barren Wilderness, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 29. 17. and seat of Wild-Beasts, as 2 <ns0:hi>Ki<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> 14. 9. Which latter sense seems more agreeable, both to the op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />position which is here tacitly made between this Mountain and <ns0:hi>the mountain of myrrhe,</ns0:hi> and to the quality of the other mountains here joined with <ns0:hi>Lebanon,</ns0:hi> and to the last clause of the verse.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> Spouse <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This is the first time that Christ gives her this name, which he now doth both to encourage and oblige her to go with him.</ns0:note>, with me from Lebanon: look <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To the place to which I invite thee to go, which from those high Mountains thou maist easily behold, the sight of which will certainly enflame thee with desire to go thither. He alludes to <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> his beholding the promised Land from mount <ns0:hi>Pisgah.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> from the top of Amana <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Not that <ns0:hi>Amana</ns0:hi> which divided <ns0:hi>Syria</ns0:hi> from <ns0:hi>Cilicia,</ns0:hi> which was too remote from these parts, but another of that name not far from <ns0:hi>Lebanon.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, from the top of Shenir <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 3. 9.</ns0:note> and Hermon <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which may be the names of two tops of the same Mountain, as <ns0:hi>Horeb</ns0:hi> & <ns0:hi>Sinai</ns0:hi> seem to have been. Or, <ns0:hi>Shenir,</ns0:hi> or (the copulative, <ns0:hi>and,</ns0:hi> being put disjunctively for <ns0:hi>or,</ns0:hi> as it is in many places, which have been observed before) <ns0:hi>Hermon,</ns0:hi> for this Mountain is called both <ns0:hi>Shenir</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Hermon, Deut.</ns0:hi> 3. 9. and the lat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter name, <ns0:hi>Hermon,</ns0:hi> may be added to the former, as being better known to the Israelites.</ns0:note>, from the li<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons dens, from the mountains of the leopards <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">From these or other such like Moun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tains, which are inhabited by Lions and Leopards. Which seems to be added as an Argument to move the Spouse to go with him, because the places where now she was, were not only barren, but also dangerous, as being the Habitations of Tyrants and Persecu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tors, and wild or salvage People, who are oft described by the names of wild Beasts, whose natures they have, and whose pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctices they imitate.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
